newsitem.title: USA: Jury selection begins in N.J. Megan's Law case.
newsitem.headline: Jury selection begins in N.J. Megan's Law case.

text.p: Attorneys began questioning hundreds of potential jurors Monday in the trial of a convicted sex offender accused of killing a 7-year-old child, prompting passage of the so-called Megan's Law.

Jesse Timmendequas is accused of luring Megan Kanka into his home, raping and strangling her in July 1994 in Hamilton Township, a working-class suburb of Trenton, New Jersey. Her body was found two miles away after a two-day search.
Timmendequas, 34, faces the death penalty if convicted.
He had been convicted twice of sex offences, unbeknownst to his neighbours, and their outrage prompted the law designed to alert communities when convicted sex offenders move in.

Defence attorneys say the extensive publicity, which has prompted similar laws nationwide, will make it difficult for Timmendequas to get a fair trial. They argue that while legal guidelines often severely restrict juries from learning about defendants' prior criminal records, jurors would know because of Megan's Law that this defendant had previous convictions.

Because of publicity surrounding the case, they also say finding a panel of impartial jurors could take longer than trying the case itself. Jury selection could take four to six months, they say. Testimony, which is expected to last a matter of weeks, is not scheduled to begin until May.

Lawyers began questioning the first pool of 300 people in Mercer County Superior Court in an effort to seat the panel of 12 jurors and four alternates. Potential jurors were given a 36-page questionnaire and were to be quizzed by Superior Court Judge Andrew Smithson on what they know about the case and whether they can be impartial.
The judge has indicated he would not bar jurors for knowing about Megan's Law, which requires convicted sex offenders to register with local authorities when they move to an area.
Defence attorneys say their client's criminal record was widely discussed in public during the campaign for the law led by the dead child's parents, Maureen and Richard Kanka.
The defence had sought to move the trial out of Mercer County because of publicity but the judge decided instead to pick a jury from neighbouring Hunterdon County.
Megan's Law is itself in legal limbo. A series of rulings have given New Jersey the power to require sex offenders to register with authorities but not to notify the public.

Critics argue Megan's Law violates rights guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution by punishing criminals after they have served their prison sentence. The status of New Jersey's Megan's Law is currently before a federal appeals court.
